one_paragraph_summary: Following De Lima's exclusion from the JBC's chief justice short list, Panganiban explains the legal distinctions and delivers institutional verdicts. De Lima prudently retracted her conspiracy accusation after Rep. Tupas (a Palace ally) clarified that the JBC applied its existing uniform rule on 'regular administrative cases': Herbosa's disbarment case was already dismissed; Jardeleza's was at an initial stage with no prima facie finding; only when the SC refers a disbarment complaint to the IBP does the case become 'regular.' De Lima can still challenge the rule in the SC or seek its amendment as an ex officio JBC member -- though the 15-day publication requirement of EO 200 made any mid-vacancy amendment moot. The author offers consolation: De Lima may be 'pruned, tested and prepared for an office higher than the chief magistracy.' He salutes the JBC for its finest hour in 25 years: first three outsiders in its short list history; first requirement of SALN, ITR, and bank waivers for all candidates; psycho-neuro tests not waived for sitting justices; and published voting tally (six of 19 candidates received zero votes). Special tribute to Ret. Justice Aurora Lagman -- unconfirmed JBC member -- who voted courageously despite political, peer, and rank disadvantages. Had Sen. Drilon agreed to be vetted, he would have been a shoo-in -- but he cited delicadeza ('of the rarest kind') about gunning for the post just vacated by the CJ he helped oust. The column closes with the author's institutional prescription: the ideal CJ-President relationship is not comfort and coziness but 'creative tension amid mutual cooperation' -- that is how checks and balances best thrive.
